transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Since my wife’s dementia diagnosis, I feel like I’m not coping well with all the changes and I’m reacting to every little thing like it’s a crisis. I'm just hoping to find a better way to handle everything that has been thrown my way lately.
Do you feel that these feelings of distress started specifically in response to your wife's diagnosis, or have you felt this way for a long time, even before these recent life changes?

These feelings are definitely new and started right after my wife's diagnosis and my work hours got cut about five months ago. Before all of this happened, I didn't feel this way at all and was generally able to take things in stride. It really only began once our lives were turned upside down.
Beyond your feelings of distress, have these changes in your life led to significant difficulties in your daily functioning, such as trouble at work or problems managing your home responsibilities?

Yes, these changes have definitely impacted my daily life. I've completely stopped going to my walking club and my church volunteer group because I'm so preoccupied. Even when I'm at work, I find myself highly distracted and constantly double-checking things in my head about my wife's care instead of focusing on my job.
Would you say that your level of distress is clearly disproportionate to the severity of these life changes, or do you feel your reactions are understandable given the circumstances?

While the overall situation with my wife's health and my job is definitely hard, my daily reactions to minor things feel completely out of proportion. I find myself treating every small hiccup, like a misplaced pill or a new bill, as an absolute crisis. It feels like I'm on constant alert instead of just taking things in stride like I used to.
Besides feeling constantly on alert, have you noticed any symptoms such as persistent low mood, loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, or significant changes in your sleep or appetite?

I have definitely lost interest in things I used to enjoy, and I've stopped going to my walking club and church volunteer group because I'm so preoccupied with my wife's care. I haven't noticed any major changes in my sleep or appetite, and it feels more like being constantly tense and on edge rather than having a persistent low mood.
When you feel like you are in a crisis, do you primarily experience physical symptoms of anxiety, such as a racing heart, muscle tension, or feeling like you are about to panic?

I haven't really noticed specific physical symptoms like a racing heart or feeling like I'm about to panic. It is more that I just feel generally tense, on edge, and mentally on constant alert all the time.
Do you find that your primary distress manifests more as feeling anxious and on edge, or does it feel more like a sense of sadness, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness?

It definitely feels much more like being constantly anxious, tense, and on high alert, as if every little thing is a major crisis. I don't really feel sad, tearful, or hopeless. It's just this constant state of worry and tension about managing everything.
Since these symptoms began five months ago, have they been present every day, or do you have periods where you feel completely back to your normal self?

These feelings have been pretty constant and persistent over the last five months rather than coming and going. I haven't really had any periods where I felt completely back to my normal self, because the worries about my wife's care and my work are always on my mind and keeping me on edge.
